newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine closes down one Chernobyl reactor.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine closes down one Chernobyl reactor.

text.p: Ukraine closed one of the two working reactors at the Chernobyl nuclear power staion on Saturday, taking a big step towards keeping promises to shut the site of the world's biggest nuclear accident by the year 2000.
"Everything went to schedule. Reactor number one was shut down at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT)," Sergei Parashin said by telephone from the Chernobyl plant, about 140 km (90 miles) from Kiev.

Ukraine has promised to close the whole Chernobyl station by 2000 in exchange for some $3.1 billion in grants and credits from the Group of Seven industrialised states. Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said in April one reactor would close this year.
"This event was not very joyful for us but we are fulfilling what we promised to the West," Parashin said, adding the state of the reactor would be studied for several months.
Plant officials have said that once the reactor has cooled down, the nuclear fuel will be removed.
The shutdown leaves the station with just one working reactor, number three.
Reactor number two was closed after a fire in the control room in 1991. The fourth reactor exploded in 1986, sending a radioactive cloud across much of Europe.
Ukraine says the disaster caused at least 4,300 deaths and the ruined reactor is buried in a concrete sarcophagus, which is itself in need of repair.

However, industry officials have criticised the closure plan and, anxious about how to provide the former Soviet republic with electricity in the winter, have drawn up contingency plans to reopen the second reactor.
Power cuts are already common in evening peak hours in the countryside during the winter.
Some industry experts have said that leaving Chernobyl with only one working reactor could also cause problems.
They say it could be hard to keep water in the station's cooling system warm to prevent pipes from breaking if the reactor was closed for repairs or after an accident.
"It is extremely dangerous to have only one reactor working in the winter," Ukraine's top Chernobyl negotiator, Yuri Kostenko, said earlier this month.
Nuclear officials have said reactor number one could be brought back on stream at any time. But Kuchma said on Friday there were no firm plans to reopen it.
"We would need hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars to rebuild it," he said. "The state does not have these funds."
The Chernobyl power station is one of five nuclear power plants in Ukraine. With two working reactors, it produced around five percent of the country's electricity.
The whole nuclear sector accounts for 40 percent of Ukraine's electricity in summer and 50 percent in winter.
